opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we're actually asking the model to do. With large language models, a big part of why they have to be so huge is that language is a compressed, symbolic record of human knowledge. To be useful, the model has to memorize an enormous amount of facts, trivia, cultural context, all the long-tail stuff people have written down. A lot of the parameters go into storing knowledge, not just into reasoning.

A world model grounded in visual intelligence is doing something different. Its core job is to understand how the physical world works: objects persist, things fall, light behaves a certain way, actions have consequences. Those regularities are, in a sense, much more compact. Physics doesn't have a long tail the way human trivia does. A cat or a toddler builds a remarkably good model of the physical world with a brain that's tiny compared to what we think of as necessary for language-level knowledge. That's a pretty strong existence proof that you don't need hundreds of billions of parameters just to get spatial and physical understanding.

The second part is that the visual signal is very rich but also very redundant. Pixels contain huge amounts of information, but most of it is predictable noise or texture that doesn't matter for understanding the scene. If you learn the right representations, focusing on structure and dynamics in a latent space instead of reconstructing every pixel, you can throw away most of that redundancy. Then the model that actually reasons about the world can be fairly small, because it operates on an abstract, compressed description rather than raw sensory data.

And practically, if we want these models to run on robots, glasses, or other devices that interact with the real world in real time, they'll have to be efficient. So I see it less as "the model can be small" and more as "the right kind of world model should be small." If you need something gigantic to capture basic physical intuition, it probably means your representation or objective isn't right yet. Scale still helps, of course, but I don't think the path to visual intelligence looks like simply copying the LLM recipe and making everything bigger.

r001.rationale: It says visual models can discard redundant pixel detail and reason over compressed representations instead of storing or reconstructing every observed detail.

r002.rationale: It mentions that objects fall and physical regularities are compact, but does not state that predicting an apple’s fall avoids solving a high-dimensional Schrödinger equation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we've conflated two very different things under the word "intelligence." Language models have to be large because text is a compressed, lossy record of human knowledge. To predict the next token well, you need to memorize an enormous amount of world knowledge: history, code, chemistry, who wrote what. That knowledge lives in the parameters, so the parameters have to be big.

Visual intelligence is a different kind of problem. The world itself is the data. A cat doesn't carry around an encyclopedia, but it has an extremely good model of physics, of objects, of what happens when it jumps. That model is not about storing facts, it's about learning the structure of the physical world: continuity, occlusion, how things move, what's likely to happen in the next half second. That structure is actually fairly low-dimensional compared to the space of all human text. There's a lot of redundancy in pixels, and a good representation throws most of it away.

So my intuition, and I'll admit it's partly intuition, is that the hard part of a visual world model is not capacity, it's representation. If you learn the right latent space, where the model reasons about objects and dynamics instead of pixels, then prediction in that space can be done with a relatively small network. A lot of the "bigness" in current video models goes into rendering every detail of every frame, which is beautiful for generation but mostly wasted if what you want is understanding and planning.

The second reason is that a world model doesn't have to know everything. It has to know enough to act. An agent in a kitchen doesn't need to model the economy of France. It needs local, grounded, predictive knowledge, and that can be updated through interaction rather than baked in at pretraining. So you can imagine a modest core model that's very good at perception and short-horizon prediction, paired with memory and tools for the long-tail knowledge. That's closer to how biological systems work, and I think it's where the efficient path lies.

I'm not saying scale won't help. It always helps a bit. But I suspect that for vision, the returns from getting the representation and the learning objective right will dwarf the returns from adding parameters, and that's a very different scaling story than the one we've seen in language.

r001.rationale: The response says pixels contain substantial redundancy, a good representation discards most of it, and modeling every frame detail is largely wasted for understanding and planning. This communicates that the trained model need not retain every observed detail.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an apple falling, a Schrödinger equation, or an equivalent contrast about avoiding a highly dimensional physics calculation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the visual world has a lot of structure. If you look at a video, consecutive frames are highly redundant. Objects persist, their motion is usually continuous, and the same physical rules apply across many different situations. You don’t necessarily need to memorize every possible scene; you need to learn the underlying regularities that generate those scenes.

So a model might observe a very high-dimensional signal but represent the important state of the world quite compactly: what objects are there, how they relate, and how they might change. Once you have that representation, predicting what happens next may not require an enormous model.

Of course, that’s a hypothesis, not a guarantee. Learning that representation could still require a lot of data and computation. But I wouldn’t assume that because the visual input is huge, the model itself has to be huge. The question is how much of that input you actually need to understand and predict.

r001.rationale: The response says a model need not memorize every possible scene and can represent the important state compactly, conveying that it need not store every observed detail.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an apple falling, a Schrödinger equation, or avoiding a high-dimensional quantum calculation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the visual world has a lot of structure and redundancy. If you look at a video, consecutive frames are incredibly similar. Objects persist, and the way they move is constrained. You don’t necessarily need a huge model to represent all those pixels independently. You need a good representation of the underlying state and how it changes.

So the complexity of the input is not necessarily the complexity of the model you need. A million pixels might be explained by a few objects, their geometry, and their interactions. If we can learn that structure, a relatively compact model could potentially predict what happens next.

Of course, that’s a hypothesis, not a claim that scaling doesn’t matter. Learning those representations could still require a lot of data and computation. But I wouldn’t assume that a capable world model has to be enormous just because the visual input is enormous. The representation and the learning objective may matter as much as the parameter count.

r001.rationale: The response says a model need not represent every pixel independently and can instead learn a compact representation of underlying state and changes.
